abstract: Bile acids are liver-derived signaling molecules that can be found in the brain, but their role there remains largely unknown. We found increased brain chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) in mice with absent 12α-hydroxylase ( Cyp8b1 ), a bile acid synthesis enzyme. In these Cyp8b1 −/− , and in W t mice administered CDCA, stroke infarct area was reduced. Elevated glutamate-induced excitotoxicity mediated by aberrant N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) overactivation contributes to neuronal death in ischemic stroke. We found reduced glutamate-induced excitotoxicity in neurons from Cyp8b1 −/− and CDCA-treated W t mice. CDCA decreased NMDAR-mediated excitatory post-synaptic currents by reducing over-activation of NMDAR subunit GluN2B in W t brains. Synaptic NMDAR activity was also decreased in Cyp8b1 −/− brains. Expression and synaptic distribution of GluN2B were unaltered in Cyp8b1 −/− mice, suggesting CDCA may directly antagonize GluN2B-containing NMDARs. Supporting our findings, in a case-control cohort of acute ischemic stroke patients, we found lower circulatory CDCA. Together, our data suggest that CDCA, acting in the liver-brain axis, decreases GluN2B-containing NMDAR overactivation, contributing to neuroprotection in stroke.

Materials and Methods
Mouse maintenance
All mouse experiments were approved by the Biomedical Sciences Institute, Singapore, institutional animal care committee, and received care as outlined in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All experiments used male mice, housed in 12 h light/dark cycles with ad libitum access to water and food (1324_modified, Altromin GmbH & Co). All animals within a group were randomly assigned, and all analyses were performed during the light cycle, by experimenters blind to the genotypes and treatment group. Study design and reporting followed the ARRIVE guidelines. Sample sizes were determined based on previous studies, and no animals were excluded. For in vivo CDCA administration, 12-week old male

Antibiotic treatment
Male

16

The antibiotics treated group was administered an antibiotic cocktail consisting of cephalothin (2 mg/ml, Sigma-Aldrich) plus neomycin (2 mg/ml, Sigma-Aldrich) in the drinking water, freshly prepared every day, for 7 days. In parallel, the nontreated group received plain water for 7 days. After the 7-day treatment, blood was collected by orbital sinus bleeding from mice fasted for 4 h. Plasma was isolated and stored at −80°C until its use for BA analyses. Mice were terminally anesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) solution (intraperitoneally). Brains were dissected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen after transcardial perfusion of the mice with 1xPBS to remove blood from the brain blood vessels and to avoid possible contamination with circulating BAs. Brain tissue was used for BA analyses and for gene expression analysis.

Neuronal cell culture and cytotoxicity assay

Mouse bile acid measurements
BAs were analyzed as described (
22
) in plasma and brains from mice that were fasted for 4 h. For plasma isolation, blood was drawn from the saphenous vein. Mice were then anaesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) and transcardially perfused with 1 × PBS. Brains were dissected and snap frozen. BAs were analyzed by ultra performance liquid chromatography electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry in multiple reactions monitoring (MRM) mode (UPLC-MRM/MS, Genome BC Proteomics Center, University of Victoria, Canada) as follows:
Plasma: 30 μl plasma, 30 μl internal standards and 240 μl of MeOH-acetonitrile (1:1) were mixed, vortexed, sonicated in an ice-water bath, and centrifuged. The supernatant was subjected to reversed-phase solid phase extraction (SPE) using Strata-X SPE cartridges (60 mg/1 ml). BAs were eluted with 1 ml x 2 of methanol-acetonitrile (1:1). The fractions were dried in a nitrogen evaporator, dissolved in 120 μl of 50% methanol, and 20 μl was injected for UPLC-MRM/MS.
Brain: Mice were anaesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) and transcardially perfused with 1 × PBS. Brains were dissected and snap frozen. Each brain was precisely weighed and placed in a 2 ml homogenizing tube. Water was added to each tube to make 3 μl/mg tissue, followed by tissue homogenization on a MM 400 mill mixer. After centrifugation, 14 μl/mg tissue of acetonitrile containing 0.05 mg/ml BHT was added and samples homogenized, and sonicated in an ice-water bath for 3 min. After centrifugation, 1 ml of supernatant (equivalent to 100 mg tissue) was mixed with 25 μl internal standard solution and subjected to phospholipid depletion-SPE. Flow-through fractions were pooled, dried in a nitrogen evaporator, reconstituted in 100 μl of 50% methanol, and 20 μl was injected for UPLC-MRM/MS. Samples were analyzed in an Agilent 1290-UHPLC coupled to a Sciex-4000 QTRAP mass spectrometer which was operated in multiple-reaction monitoring (MRM) mode with negative-ion detection. A Waters BEH-C18 column (2.1 mm I.D. × 15 cm, 1.7 μm) was used for LC separation with a mobile phase of (A) 0.01% formic acid (FA) in water and (B) 0.01% FA in acetonitrile for binary-solvent gradient elution. A standard mix containing reference substances of all the targeted BAs was dissolved in 50% methanol at 10 nmol/ml each. This solution (S1) was further diluted step by step at a same dilution ratio of 1–4 (v/v) with the same solvent to have standard solutions of S2 to S10. Subsequently, 50 μl of S1 to S10 each was mixed with 50 μl of an internal standard solution containing 14 Deuterium-labeled bile acid analogues. Subsequently, 20 μl of each solution was injected to run UPLC-(−)ESI-MRM/MS. Linear calibration curves were constructed using analyte-to-internal standard peak area ratios (As/Ai) versus molar concentrations (nmol/ml) of each bile acid. Data were normalized to the average of control mice (nontreated or
Cyp8b1
+/+
mice) and presented as fold change in figures. Raw bile acid concentrations were also presented in tables. Secondary BA correspond to the sum of deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, ω-muricholic acid, taurodeoxycholic acid, and Tauro ω-muricholic acid. Total of 12α-hydroxylated BA correspond to the sum of cholic acid, DCA, taurocholic acid, and TDCA. Total of non-12α-hydroxylated BA correspond to the sum of CDCA, ursodeoxycholic acid, αMCA, βMCA, ω-muricholic acid, tauro chenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA), TUDCA, tauro α-muricholic acid, TβMCA, and Tauro ω-muricholic acid.

Transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) was carried out as previously described (
23
). Male mice (4.5–6 months) were anesthetized with isoflurane. An incision was made in the neck of the mice and the left common carotid artery (LCCA) was isolated and ligated using a 1.5 cm long 0/7 silk suture. The left external carotid artery was separated and a second ligature was made. The left internal carotid artery (LICA) was isolated and ligated with 7/0 silk suture. A small incision was made in the LCCA before it bifurcates and a 0.21 mm MCAO silicone-rubber coated nylon monofilament (Doccol Corporation) was introduced into the LICA for 9–10 mm, to occlude the origin of the left middle cerebral artery at the circle of Willis. The ligature on the LICA was closed to fix the filament in position. After 1 h of artery occlusion, the nylon monofilament and common carotid artery ligature were removed to initiate brain reperfusion. The retractors were removed and the muscle layer and the two fat bodies returned to the physiological position. The skin was closed with three separated metallic clips and the mouse placed on its left side under the infrared light until awake. Mice were sacrificed 24 h post-MCAO, and brains isolated and sectioned in 2 mm coronal sections. Lesion area was identified by incubating brain sections with 2% 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS at 37°C for 5 min, followed by washing. Images were captured and infarct area quantified using ImageJ (
https://imagej.net/ij/
). Data are expressed as % of infarct area/total brain area.

The retractors were removed and the muscle layer and the two fat bodies returned to the physiological position. The skin was closed with surgical glue and the mouse placed on its left side on a heating pad until awake. Mice were sacrificed 24 h post-MCAO, and brains isolated and sectioned in 2 mm coronal sections. Lesion area was identified by incubating brain sections with 2% 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS at 37°C for 5 min, followed by washing. Images were captured and infarct area quantified using ImageJ. Data are expressed as % of infarct area/total brain area.

Neurotransmitter quantification
Neurotransmitter quantification was conducted by Metabolon. Glutamate and glutamate metabolites were evaluated in

Several recovery standards were added prior to the first step in the extraction process for quality control (QC) purposes. To remove protein, dissociate small molecules bound to protein or trapped in the precipitated protein matrix, and to recover chemically diverse metabolites, proteins were precipitated with methanol under vigorous shaking for 2 min (Glen Mills Geno Grinder 2000) followed by centrifugation. Samples were placed briefly on a TurboVap® (Zymark) to remove the organic solvent. Several types of controls were analyzed in concert with the experimental samples: a pooled matrix sample generated by taking a small volume of each experimental sample (or alternatively, use of a pool of well-characterized human plasma) served as a technical replicate throughout the data set; extracted water samples served as process blanks; and a cocktail of QC standards that were carefully chosen not to interfere with the measurement of endogenous compounds were spiked into every analyzed sample, and allowed instrument performance monitoring and aided chromatographic alignment. Samples were analyzed in a Waters ACQUITY UPLC and a Thermo Fisher Scientific Q-Exactive high resolution/accurate mass spectrometer interfaced with a heated electrospray ionization (HESI-II) source and Orbitrap mass analyzer operated at 35,000 mass resolution. The sample extract was reconstituted in solvents compatible to each of the four methods. Each reconstitution solvent contained a series of standards at fixed concentrations to ensure injection and chromatographic consistency. One aliquot was analyzed using acidic positive ion conditions, chromatographically optimized for more hydrophilic compounds. In this method, the extract was gradient eluted from a C18 column (Waters UPLC BEH C18-2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm) using water and methanol, containing 0.05% perfluoropentanoic acid and 0.1% FA. Another aliquot was also analyzed using acidic positive ion conditions. However, it was chromatographically optimized for more hydrophobic compounds. In this method, the extract was gradient eluted from the same afore mentioned C18 column using methanol, acetonitrile, water, 0.05% perfluoropentanoic acid, and 0.01% FA and was operated at an overall higher organic content. Another aliquot was analyzed using basic negative ion optimized conditions using a separate dedicated C18 column. The basic extracts were gradient eluted from the column using methanol and water with 6.5 mM ammonium bicarbonate at pH 8. The fourth aliquot was analyzed via negative ionization following elution from a hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography column (Waters UPLC BEH Amide 2.1 × 150 mm, 1.7 μm) using a gradient consisting of water and acetonitrile with 10 mM ammonium formate, pH 10.8. In order to correct variation resulting from instrument interday tuning differences, each compound was corrected in run-day blocks by registering the medians to equal one and normalizing each data point proportionately.

24
). The tissue blocks were cryoprotected in increasing concentrations of glycerol (30 min in 10%, 30 min in 20%, and overnight in 30% at 4°C) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer and then frozen in a cryofixation unit (Reichert KF80, Vienna, Austria) filled with propane which was cooled down by liquid nitrogen. The tissue pieces were placed in Reichert capsules in a flow through chamber filled with 1.5% uranyl acetate diluted in anhydrous methanol in a precooled chamber (−90°C) in a Reichert automatic freeze substitution unit (Leica Microsystems). Following 30 h at −90°C, the temperature was raised by 4°C increments per hour from −90 to −45°C. The tissue pieces were rinsed with anhydrous methanol and infiltrated with Lowicryl HM20 resin (Polysciences Inc., Warrington, PA; Cat#15924) at a temperature of −45°C. Infiltration in 1:1 and 2:1 methanol to pure Lowicryl lasted for 2 h each, followed by 2 h and then overnight in pure Lowicryl. The Reichert capsules were moved to Lowicryl-filled gelatin capsules and then transferred to another container filled with ethanol. The resin/tissue was polymerized with UV-light for 24 h at −45°C. The temperature was increased by 5°C increments to 0°C where it was polymerized for further 35 h. Ultrathin sections (90 nm) were cut with a diamond knife (Diatome ultra 45°, Diatome) on an ultramicrotome (Reichert Ultracut S-2.GA-E−12/92, Leica Microsystems) and placed on coated (Coat-Quick “G”) nickel grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences, G300-Ni).
Postembedding immunogold labeling was carried out by incubating the sections in Tris buffered saline with Tween20 (TBST, pH 7.4) containing 50 mM glycine (10 min) and in TBST containing 5% normal goat serum (GSA) (10 min) to neutralize free aldehyde groups and blocking nonspecific antibody binding sites, respectively. The sections were incubated with anti-GluN2B (1:50 in 5% new-born goat serum in TBS with 0.1% Triton X-100) for 2 h at room temperature. The sections were rinsed and immersed in TBST (10 min), before they were incubated in goat anti-rabbit IgG colloidal gold-secondary antibody 1:20, in 5% new-born goat serum and 1 mg/ml PEG in TBST for 90 min. The sections were then rinsed with distilled water and poststained with 2% uranyl acetate (90 s) and 0.3% lead citrate (90 s). Uranyl acetate and lead citrate were removed with distilled water, and sections were left to dry completely before use in the electron microscope. All sections were labeled blinded on a grid support plate at room temperature.
Electron micrographs were acquired using a transmission electron microscope (Tecnai G2 Spirit, FEI Company) operating at high tension (80 kV) with a 430,00× magnification. Electron micrographs were obtained at random from the middle layer of the stratum radiatum of the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus. Immunolabeling was quantified as number of gold particles/μm of membrane length in asymmetric synapses. Asymmetric synapses in this location are well-defined glutamatergic synapses, where the presynaptic element is the nerve ending of the Schaffer collateral neurons they originate from. Excitatory synapses were identified by the presence of two closely aligned membranes with a synaptic cleft, a prominent postsynaptic density (PSD) and circular synaptic membrane-orientated vesicles at the presynaptic side. Only synaptic profiles with clearly visible synaptic membranes and a PSD were selected for quantitative analysis. The images were quantified by ImageJ. For the quantification of PSD, the plugin “distance to path” was used in ImageJ, to study the linear density of gold particles along the PSD (
25
). The segmented line tool was used to outline the region of interest, PSD, and the gold particles were marked with the multipoint tool. This was done to every synapse that was included from the micrographs. The outlined path and the points were then saved with a corresponding dtp file containing the coordinate information. All micrographs with the coordinates of the PSD and the gold particles were then run with the python component of the software tool to get the data from each synapse. The spatial resolution is the resolution for the postembedding immunogold technique and must be determined to distinguish whether gold particles are more likely to being attached to the postsynaptic membrane. Theoretically, the resolution of this technique depends on the distance between the epitope and the center of the gold particle. This distance represents the radius of the gold particle and the diameter of both antibodies (primary and secondary). Briefly, 12 nm gold particles were used, and with a radius of 6 nm in addition to the length of both the primary and the secondary antibody, 8 nm each, the spatial resolution was set to 22 nm in python. The program produced information of all gold particles within 22 nm of distance to the PSD line, and the length of the PSD. The output was produced in excel files. The columns used from the excel-file were “path length” and “particles within 22 nm of path”. With this information, linear gold particle density was calculated for each synapse. The data were then converted from nm to μm. The gold particle density (GPD) was quantified as number of gold particles per μm along the plasma membrane. After quantification, the data were imported into SPSS for further statistical analysis (
https://www.ibm.com/products/spss-statistics
). Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27. The Shapiro-Wilk normality test was performed to determine normal data distribution. Normally distributed data were analyzed with an Independent Samples
t
test to compare the two groups. Nonnormally distributed data were analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests. Statistical significance level was set to
P
< 0.05. Normally distributed data were presented as mean ± SD while nonnormally distributed data were presented as median ± SEM.
Validation study in humans
A prospective case-control study evaluating the association between serum CDCA levels and ischemic stroke risk was conducted at the National University Hospital (NUH) Singapore. A total of 57 adult patients admitted with acute ischemic stroke and 54 age- and ethnicity-matched controls, reviewed at the same center for nonneurological causes, were recruited. All subjects were Chinese, and between the ages 40 and 61 years. The study protocol was approved by the Singapore National Healthcare Group Domain Specific Review Board (DSRB2016/00210 and DSRB2022/00395). All participants gave written informed consent before study participation.
Cases
Cases were patients with acute ischemic stroke of atherosclerotic origin confirmed on brain parenchymal and neurovascular imaging. Brain parenchymal imaging was performed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and neurovascular imaging was performed with computed tomography angiography or magnetic resonance angiography. Patients with haemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke of nonatherosclerotic origin, a history of chronic liver disease or liver cirrhosis, or who were unable to give informed consent to participate in the study were excluded.
Controls
The control cohort comprised community-dwelling adults seen at the outpatient clinic for nonneurological causes. Exclusion criteria for the control participants was a known history of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, systolic, and diastolic blood pressure higher than 150 and 100 mm Hg, respectively, LDL-C >4.1 mmol/L, hemoglobin A1c >8.0%, a history of chronic liver disease or liver cirrhosis, and self-reported chronic kidney disease.
Blood sampling and bile acid measurements
Blood samples were collected and centrifuged within 1 h at 4°C for 10 min at 3,550
g
. Serum samples were stored at −80°C until use. Bile acids were analyzed using ultra high performance liquid chromatography electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry in multiple reactions monitoring mode (UHPLC-MRM/MS). Bile acid standards were from Merck, Singapore, and stable isotope internal standards from Cayman Chemical (Ann Arbor, MI) or Cambridge Isotope Laboratories (Tewksbury, MA). Subsequently, 25 μl plasma, 25 μl internal standards (3–5 μg/L), and 180 μl acetonitrile containing 0.1% FA were mixed for 10 min with the Agilent Bravo automated liquid handling platform set at 1,000 rpm/min and centrifuged at 2,270
g
for 50 min at 4°C. The supernatant was subjected to reversed-phase SPE using a Waters Ostro™ 96-well plate 25 mg SPE column (Cat no: 18600518). Nitrogen gas attached to a positive pressure manifold 96 processor (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) was used at 6 psi to obtain phospholipid-free supernatant. This was loaded into the auto-sampler of the Agilent 1,290 Infinity-UHPLC coupled to a 6495C triple quadrupole (QqQ) mass spectrometer which was operated in MRM mode with negative-ion detection. Chromatographic separation was achieved with a Restek’s Raptor C18 HPLC column (2.1 × 50 mm, pore size 90 Å, 1.8 μm, Cat # 9304252). The mobile phase contained 5 mM ammonium acetate in water (Solvent A) and methanol/acetonitrile 1:1 (Solvent B). The flow rate was 0.5 ml/min. The injection volume was 10 μl per sample. The gradient was: linear 35%–40% B from 0.0 to 1.0 min, linear 40%–45% B from 1.0 to 2.5 min, linear 45%–50% B from 2.5 to 7.5 min, linear 50%–55% B from 7.5 to 8.6 min, linear 55%–80% B from 8.6 to 9.7 min, linear 80%–95% B from 9.7 to 9.9 min, isocratic 95% B from 9.9 to 10.5 min, linear 95%-35% B from 10.5 to 10.51 min, and isocratic 35% B from 10.51 to 12.00 min. All samples were analyzed in random order. MRM chromatogram acquisitions and quantifications were performed using the Agilent MassHunter Workstation Acquisition (10.0.127;
https://www.agilent.com/en-us/products/software-informatics/masshunter-suite/
) and Quantitative Analysis (10.1.733). Chromatographic peak integration and batch correction were performed as described (
26
). Deuterated stable isotopic internal standards were used for CDCA, GCDCA, and TCDCA quantification. Deuterated TCDCA was used as structural analogue internal standard for DCA and UCDA quantification. Linear calibration curves were constructed using analyte-to-internal standard peak area response ratios (As/Ai) versus molar concentrations (nmol/ml) of each BA. Relative quantification and tertiles comparisons were based on the validated response ratios.
Statistical analyses
Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (
https://www.graphpad.com
). All values are mean ± SEM. A nominal
P
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Normal distribution of data were assessed using Shapiro-Wilk or D’Agostino and Pearson tests. Normally distributed data were analyzed using unpaired students
t
-tests. Nonparametric data were analyzed using Mann-Whitney
U
-tests. For correlations, Spearman analysis for nonparametric data were used. For multiple comparisons, One-way ANOVA was used, followed by Kruskal–Wallis posttests. Grubbs' test was performed to identify and exclude outliers. All authors had access to the study data and have reviewed and approved the final manuscript.
Human cohort data were analyzed using R (4.2.2;
https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base
). The “tidyverse” package (
https://www.tidyverse.org
) was used for data wrangling and the “ggplot2”, and “forestplot” packages were used for visualization. Logistic regression analysis was performed using the glm (equation, family = binomial (link = "logit")) base R function. Convergence of maximum likelihood estimations was reached for all regression models.

The cross-organ signaling between the liver and brain has garnered recent attention. One pathway that connects liver and brain is the vagus nerve in the autonomic nervous system. Liver derived factors such as bile acids (BAs) form another pathway linking the brain and liver (
1
). BAs are amphipathic end products of cholesterol metabolism that aid in the solubilization, digestion, and absorption of lipids and lipid-soluble nutrients in the gastrointestinal system (
2
). The discovery that BAs and their receptors are present in the brain during normal physiological conditions (
3
,
4
,
5
) raise the possibility that central control of metabolism and neuronal function can be regulated by BAs. Liver-derived BAs can enter the brain through the blood–brain barrier (
6
), again suggesting that BAs may act in the liver-brain axis to modulate neurological function. However, how BAs modulate brain function remains unclear.
In humans, liver generates two primary BAs, the 12α
-
hydroxylated BA cholic acid (CA), and the non-12α
-
hydroxylated BA chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) (
2
) (
Fig. 1
A). In mice, CDCA is converted to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and muricholic acids (MCAs) which are also primary BAs. In humans, UDCA is a secondary BA, generated through the action of gut microbiota. In the final step in the liver BA synthesis, the BAs are conjugated with predominantly glycine in humans, and taurine in mice, before entering the bloodstream (
7
). In both humans and mice, CA and CDCA levels are tightly controlled by sterol 12α-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450 family 8 subfamily B member 1, CYP8B1), which synthesizes 12α-hydroxylated BAs, including CA (
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
) (
Fig. 1
A). In the absence of CYP8B1, a substantial decrease in CA, and a compensatory increase in CDCA and its non-12α-hydroxylated BA derivatives are observed (
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
).

The neutral bile acid synthesis pathway is the major pathway of BA synthesis and occurs in the liver. Cytochrome P450 Family 8 Subfamily B Member 1 (CYP8B1) generates the primary BA cholic acid (CA). In the absence of CYP8B1, CA is reduced, and the primary BA chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) is increased. Before secretion from the liver, primary BAs are conjugated with either glycine or taurine. (B) Brain secondary BAs, which are derived solely from intestinal gut bacterial function, are reduced in WT mice administered antibiotics. (C) The primary bile acid cholic acid (CA) is decreased, and tauro conjugated CDCA (TCDCA), as well as its derivatives tauro α-muricholic acid (TαMCA) and tauro β-muricholic acid (TβMCA) trended toward increase in brain upon antibiotic administration. (D) Plasma secondary BAs are reduced in antibiotics-administered

mice. (E) CA is decreased, and TCDCA, TαMCA, and TβMCA trended toward increase in antibiotics-administered plasma. (F) Brain BAs are strongly correlated with plasma BAs (r
s
= 0.84) post antibiotic administration. (G) Antibiotic administration does not alter brain mRNA expression of the BA synthesis enzymes
Cyp8b1
,
Cyp27a1
and
Cyp7b1
. mRNA expression was normalized to
Gapdh
. Data are shown as average ± SEM, and assessed using Mann-Whitney

-tests. ND = not detected. r

Although not much is known about the function of BAs in the brain, administration of tauro-ursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) to mouse models of neurodegenerative disorders reduced their pathologic phenotypes (
12
). CYP27A1, a BA synthesis enzyme, is widely distributed, showing highest expression in the liver, and is also expressed in the brain (
biogps.org
). Its absence results in brain cholesterol accumulation (
13
), suggesting that de novo BA synthesis may also occur in the brain. In humans, mutations in
CYP27A1
result in almost absent CDCA synthesis, leading to cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX), a rare neurodegenerative disorder (
13
). Although several BAs, including the intestinal derivatives of CDCA, have been tested as treatments for CTX, CDCA administration is the only effective treatment for the neurological symptoms in patients with CTX (
14
,
15
). However, the mechanism by which CDCA reduces CTX symptoms remains unknown. Together, these data suggest that BAs, particularly CDCA, may have the potential to directly regulate neuronal function. Thus, further clarification of the functional roles of this BA in neurophysiology is required.
Here, we investigated the capacity of CDCA to act as a signaling molecule in the liver–brain axis by assessing its effects on neuronal function in both mice in which deleted
Cyp8b1
led to increased brain CDCA, and in
W
t
mice administered CDCA.
Materials and Methods
Mouse maintenance
All mouse experiments were approved by the Biomedical Sciences Institute, Singapore, institutional animal care committee, and received care as outlined in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All experiments used male mice, housed in 12 h light/dark cycles with ad libitum access to water and food (1324_modified, Altromin GmbH & Co). All animals within a group were randomly assigned, and all analyses were performed during the light cycle, by experimenters blind to the genotypes and treatment group. Study design and reporting followed the ARRIVE guidelines. Sample sizes were determined based on previous studies, and no animals were excluded. For in vivo CDCA administration, 12-week old male
W
t
C57BL/6N
mice were fed standard diet containing 1% CDCA (w/w) for 7 days.
Antibiotic treatment
Male
W
t
C57BL/6N
mice (Taconic) between 13 and 15 weeks of age were submitted to a 7-day antibiotic treatment paradigm as previously described (
16
). Briefly, a total of 28 male mice from two different cohorts were randomly divided into two groups, nontreated and antibiotics treated. Mice were housed in groups of 3–4 per cage. The antibiotics treated group was administered an antibiotic cocktail consisting of cephalothin (2 mg/ml, Sigma-Aldrich) plus neomycin (2 mg/ml, Sigma-Aldrich) in the drinking water, freshly prepared every day, for 7 days. In parallel, the nontreated group received plain water for 7 days. After the 7-day treatment, blood was collected by orbital sinus bleeding from mice fasted for 4 h. Plasma was isolated and stored at −80°C until its use for BA analyses. Mice were terminally anesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) solution (intraperitoneally). Brains were dissected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen after transcardial perfusion of the mice with 1xPBS to remove blood from the brain blood vessels and to avoid possible contamination with circulating BAs. Brain tissue was used for BA analyses and for gene expression analysis.

Mixed cortical and glial cell cultures were prepared as previously described (

The cell suspension rested for 10 min at room temperature. The supernatant (avoiding the debris) was transferred into a new tube and homogenized by gentle pipetting. Neurons were plated on poly-L-lysine (Sigma-Aldrich) coated plates in the plating medium at a density of 5 × 10

A day after plating, media were replaced with fresh media, and subsequently, half the media weres replaced every 3–4 days. After 14 days in culture, cells were incubated either with 30 μM L-glutamate (Sigma-Aldrich) (
19

Cytotoxicity was evaluated in the culture media after 24 h treatment, using Pierce LDH Cytotoxicity Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following manufacturer’s protocol. For Hippocampal neurons, Hippocampi were isolated from postnatal day 0 pups in ice cold Ca

Tissues were washed thrice with dissociation medium before dissociation in 0.25% Trypsin (Gibco) for 10 min at 37°C, prior to pipetting up and down with a 5 ml serological pipet in the presence of DNase I. Trypsin was deactivated with an equal amount of fetal bovine serum and the cell suspension was passed through a 70 μm cell strainer. The resulting cell suspension was spun at 120 g for 5 min. Mouse bile acid measurements
BAs were analyzed as described (
22
) in plasma and brains from mice that were fasted for 4 h. For plasma isolation, blood was drawn from the saphenous vein. Mice were then anaesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) and transcardially perfused with 1 × PBS. Brains were dissected and snap frozen. BAs were analyzed by ultra performance liquid chromatography electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry in multiple reactions monitoring (MRM) mode (UPLC-MRM/MS, Genome BC Proteomics Center, University of Victoria, Canada) as follows:
Plasma: 30 μl plasma, 30 μl internal standards and 240 μl of MeOH-acetonitrile (1:1) were mixed, vortexed, sonicated in an ice-water bath, and centrifuged. The supernatant was subjected to reversed-phase solid phase extraction (SPE) using Strata-X SPE cartridges (60 mg/1 ml). BAs were eluted with 1 ml x 2 of methanol-acetonitrile (1:1). The fractions were dried in a nitrogen evaporator, dissolved in 120 μl of 50% methanol, and 20 μl was injected for UPLC-MRM/MS.
Brain: Mice were anaesthetized with ketamine (150 mg/kg)/xylazine (10 mg/kg) and transcardially perfused with 1 × PBS. Brains were dissected and snap frozen. Each brain was precisely weighed and placed in a 2 ml homogenizing tube. Water was added to each tube to make 3 μl/mg tissue, followed by tissue homogenization on a MM 400 mill mixer. After centrifugation, 14 μl/mg tissue of acetonitrile containing 0.05 mg/ml BHT was added and samples homogenized, and sonicated in an ice-water bath for 3 min. After centrifugation, 1 ml of supernatant (equivalent to 100 mg tissue) was mixed with 25 μl internal standard solution and subjected to phospholipid depletion-SPE. A prospective case-control study evaluating the association between serum CDCA levels and ischemic stroke risk was conducted at the National University Hospital (NUH) Singapore. Discussion
We show here that the primary bile acid CDCA reduces GluN2B-containing NMDAR overactivation that occurs during excitotoxicity, thereby decreasing neuronal death. Our findings, both in mice and humans, suggest that CDCA acts in the liver–brain axis to beneficially modulate brain neurophysiology and signaling. We also find here that absence of the BA synthesis enzyme CYP8B1 in mice increases brain CDCA levels, thus likely reducing excitotoxic neuronal cell death. In addition to stroke (
30
), neuronal excitotoxicity is a key pathological process in neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington, Alzheimer’s, and Parkinson’s diseases (
45
). Thus, our data suggest that inhibition of CYP8B1 represents a potential therapeutic avenue for protection against excitotoxicity-mediated neuronal disorders.
In our study, we have not shown
in-vivo
that the neuroprotection was caused directly by increased CDCA reducing GluN2B receptor overactivation. However, MCAO is a model of ischemic stroke. During ischemia, the lack of glucose and oxygen induces neuronal cell depolarization and glutamate release. Excessive extracellular levels of glutamate induces loss of Ca
2+
homeostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased production of reactive oxygen species, and neuronal death (
28
). Substantial evidence indicate that antagonists specifically targeting GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors (e.g. ifenprodil) reduce NMDA-induced toxicity both
in-vitro
and in
in-vivo
MCAO models (
46
). In contrast, antagonists that specifically target GluN2A-containing NMDA receptors (e.g. NVP-AAM077), either show no impact or worsen neuronal death in both
in-vitro
and
in-vivo
settings (reviewed in (
47
)). These findings suggest that the inhibition of GluN2B-containing NMDAR activity is beneficial in cases of ischemic stroke. We found in our
in-vivo
studies that elevated CDCA (either in
Cyp8b1
−/−
mice or in
W
t
mice administered CDCA) resulted in reduced lesions post MCAO. In humans, increased CDCA associated with reduced ischemic stroke. In addition, our
ex-vivo
studies show that increased CDCA reduces GluN2B-mediated EPSCs but not GluN2A-mediated EPSCs. Together, these findings suggest that increased CDCA reduces lesion size in ischemic stroke by reducing NR2B receptor over activation.
In our ethnicity- and age range-matched case-control study, we found that CDCA is significantly lower in acute ischemic stroke patients compared to controls. Other BAs besides CDCA, such as DCA and UDCA were not decreased in the cases, suggesting that any differences in sample handing in our case-control study may not have affected BA stability. To further validate our results, an ideal approach would involve studies in a longitudinal prospective cohort of healthy controls, measuring baseline CDCA levels, and monitoring for acute ischemic stroke events over an extended period. However, such a study was not feasible since it necessitated large sample sizes and prolonged follow-up durations due to the low event rate for acute ischemic stroke.
In
Cyp8b1
−/−
brains, both CDCA and TUDCA are increased. Under identical experimental conditions, our data show that CDCA significantly reduces excitotoxic neuronal death, whereas TUDCA does not. Previous studies, assessing only TUDCA, suggested that it was neuroprotective by decreasing mitochondrial depolarization, thus reducing apoptosis via a PI3K-dependent pathway (
12
). The presence of distinct chemical moieties affects the physical characteristics of BAs, leading to their individual activities as signaling molecules (
48
). Thus, it is not surprising that, compared to TUDCA, CDCA more robustly reduces glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. In line with this, of several BAs tested in vitro, CDCA and its conjugates were the most efficient antagonists of NMDAR (
20
,
49
).
Excitotoxicity-induced neuronal death in neurodegenerative diseases and ischemic stroke is mainly modulated by GluN2B-containing NMDARs (
30
,
45
). The selective blockade of GluN2B-containing NMDARs reduces ischemic cell death, while the selective blockade of GluN2A-containing NMDARs enhances neuronal death in ischemia (
50
). These findings further corroborate our data suggesting that CDCA is neuroprotective by reducing aberrant GluN2B-containing NMDAR activity.
Besides reducing aberrant NMDAR activation, CDCA may also decrease neurotoxicity via other mechanisms. CDCA is the most potent BA agonist for farnesoid X receptor (FXR) (
2
), which is found in the brain (
4
). Although the role of brain FXR is unknown,
Fxr
−/−
mice show impaired motor coordination and cognitive dysfunction (
51
). As well, ablation of FXR in mice reduced infarct volume resulting from tMCAO (
52
), suggesting that FXR signaling is deleterious in ischemic stroke. In our models, if CDCA increases FXR activity, we should have observed increased infarct volume in response to tMCAO, but we observed the opposite. Thus, in our mice, FXR signaling in the brain was likely unchanged. A reason for this may be that although CDCA agonizes FXR activity, β-MCA, which is also increased in the
Cyp8b1
−/−
brains (
supplemental Table S4
), acts as an FXR antagonist (
53
). As well, CDCA reduced amyloid-β-42 and improved cognition in an AD mouse model, suggested to be through FXR-mediated pathways (
54
). CDCA is also an agonist for Takeda G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5/GPBAR1), which is also found in brain (
5
). Hypothalamic TGR5 regulates energy expenditure and obesity (
55
). The CDCA-induced antagonism of NMDAR, however, was shown to be TGR5 independent (
20
).
In addition to neurons, astrocytes, whose foot processes make close contact with neurons, also contain NMDARs (
56
). Astrocytes release gliotransmitters, including glutamate, in a feedback process regulating neuronal function (
57
). Overactivation of astrocytic NMDARs modulates AD, with Aβ increasing GluN2A and GluN2B expression in astrocytes, but only in the presence of neurons (
58
). Furthermore, NMDARs are also found in oligodendrocytes (
59
). Thus, detailed analyses of the effects of CDCA on NMDAR-mediated signaling in neurons, astrocytes and glia are necessary to understand the full complexity of BA-mediated regulation of NMDAR activity.
CDCA, at pharmacological concentrations, is relatively nontoxic, and its use as a therapeutic agent was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat certain liver conditions and CTX (
60
). CDCA and UDCA, found at relatively similar amounts, are the most abundant BAs in bear bile (
61
). Bear bile has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for hundreds of years, with no major adverse effects. In addition,
Cyp8b1
−/−
mice with elevated CDCA show no overt adverse phenotypes. In contrast,
Cyp8b1
−/−
mice show improved glucose tolerance (
9
), and humans heterozygous for loss of function mutations in
CYP8B1
show improved insulin sensitivity (
11
).
Cyp8b1
−/−
mice also show decreased susceptibility to atherosclerosis (
62
), and decreased hepatic steatosis (
10
). Together, these data suggest that elevated CDCA at pharmacological levels are nontoxic, and that reduced CYP8B1 maybe protective against several disorders. Our data suggest that increasing CDCA by inhibiting CYP8B1 might represent a therapeutic avenue to target brain disorders in which excitotoxicity plays a role.
